title: {{NAME}} and the Biggest Goalkeeper Ever
moral: The most surprising teammates can become your greatest allies.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a grass-green soccer jersey, dark shorts, and mud-caked green cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The brontosaurus appeared in the town park on the morning of the championship match, standing exactly where the goalposts were supposed to be.

The referee said the match was cancelled. The other team said the match was cancelled. {{NAME}}'s team looked at the enormous dinosaur, then at {{NAME}}.

"I have an idea," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
The dinosaur was, it turned out, extremely interested in the ball.

Every time it rolled toward its enormous feet, it nudged it back gently with a toe the size of a dustbin lid.

"What if," said {{NAME}} slowly, "she's the goalkeeper?"

The other team protested. But the referee, who had a sense of humour, noted that the rules technically did not specify that goalkeepers had to be human.

The dinosaur lowered her head and looked at {{NAME}} with one enormous amber eye.

"I'll give you signals," {{NAME}} told her. She blinked.

pages.content:
The match was extraordinary.

The dinosaur blocked every shot simply by existing in the goalmouth. But she also required strategic management: she only moved if {{NAME}} pointed, and she moved very slowly, so timing was everything.

{{NAME}} spent the entire match directing her like an air traffic controller, calling "left" and "right" while also playing midfield.

By the final whistle his voice was gone, his lungs were empty, and his team had won four-nil.

pages.content:
In the confusion of celebrating, {{NAME}} noticed the dinosaur was looking at him with an expression he could only describe as pleased.

He walked up to her and patted the side of her enormous nose.

She made a sound like distant thunder, then lowered her head and very gently nudged him sideways, once, the way a dog nuzzles a hand.

"Good game," said {{NAME}}.

Another distant-thunder sound. He was beginning to understand this meant you too.

pages.content:
The dinosaur wandered off at dusk, back toward the distant hills, the ground trembling softly with each step.

{{NAME}} sat on the field and watched until she disappeared.

He walked home through the quiet evening with the championship trophy under his arm, his voice still gone, his knees still grass-stained.

He was almost asleep when he heard it: a low rumble in the distance, too regular to be thunder, rolling gently through the night.

He smiled and pulled the blanket up.
